pages.title: About
pages.content:
A clinic built around the morning.

Yawara Rheumatology was founded in 2014 by Dr. Miriam Achterberg at 12 Linden Row in Harrow Quay. Having spent eleven years working in a hospital rheumatology unit, Dr. Achterberg recognized that patients living with inflammatory joint conditions needed care designed specifically around how symptoms appear in daily life. She established the clinic on the second floor of a quiet harbour-town building with lift access, creating a clinical environment organized entirely around morning symptoms, early diagnosis, and unhurried consultations.

From the beginning, the clinic's clinical method has centred on thorough objectivity and shared understanding. Every initial assessment includes a comprehensive 28-joint examination, same-morning musculoskeletal ultrasound, and targeted blood tests. Rather than leaving treatment open-ended, the clinic structured a rigorous four-step pathway: patients track a seven-day morning-stiffness diary, complete a sixty-minute first consultation, and return within ten days for an agreed one-page written treatment plan signed by both doctor and patient.

Over the years, the practice has grown to bring together a dedicated clinical team spanning rheumatologists, a rheumatology nurse specialist, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and pharmacy liaison. Care continues systematically through scheduled reviews at four, twelve, and twenty-four weeks, supported by a direct named-nurse phone line and same-morning flare-day slots. The clinic remains committed to its core founding principle: treating joint inflammation early and methodically so patients can preserve the steady shape of their day.

pages.title: Conditions
pages.content:
Rheumatoid arthritis

Swollen, warm small joints of both hands and feet with morning stiffness that lasts longer than half an hour. We check every joint, image the worst ones the same morning and agree a plan within ten days.

Psoriatic arthritis

Joint pain or a swollen finger in someone with psoriasis or nail changes. The examination looks at skin, nails and tendon attachments as well as joints.

Gout

A sudden hot, swollen joint, often the big toe. We confirm the diagnosis, explain what triggers it and agree a plan for flares and for the long term.

Axial spondyloarthritis

Back pain that is worse after rest and eases with movement, usually starting before 45. Examination, imaging and a movement programme with our physiotherapist.

Polymyalgia rheumatica

Aching and stiffness around the shoulders and hips, worst in the morning, in people over 50. Reviews are frequent at first and spaced out as things settle.

Lupus (SLE)

Joint pain with tiredness, rashes or sun sensitivity. Care is shared with your family doctor, with blood and urine checks at every review.

pages.title: Your first visit
pages.content:
Four visits, one page

1. Call & 7-day morning-stiffness diary

2. First visit, 60 min (history, 28-joint exam, ultrasound, bloods same morning)

3. Plan meeting within 10 days (one-page written plan agreed and signed by both)

4. Reviews at 4, 12 and 24 weeks, then every 3 months; one named nurse line

Bring your medicine list, any earlier scans, and the seven-day diary. The ultrasound is done on the day, in room 2.

pages.title: Team
pages.content:
Dr. Miriam Achterberg

Founder, Lead Rheumatologist. Dr. Miriam Achterberg founded Yawara Rheumatology in 2014 after eleven years in a hospital rheumatology unit. She leads diagnostic consultations, 28-joint examinations, and comprehensive long-term treatment planning.

Dr. Kofi Mensah-Lund

Rheumatologist, Musculoskeletal Ultrasound. Dr. Kofi Mensah-Lund specializes in inflammatory arthritis assessment and diagnostic musculoskeletal ultrasound. He performs point-of-care ultrasound during initial visits to evaluate joint inflammation without delay.

Ines Varga

Rheumatology Nurse Specialist. Ines Varga manages the dedicated named-nurse telephone line and coordinates ongoing care reviews for registered patients. She assists patients with flare management protocols and daily routine adjustments.

Tamsin Rehn

Physiotherapist. Tamsin Rehn leads patient rehabilitation focused on preserving joint mobility, hand function, and physical resilience. She guides individual exercise sessions and practical movement therapies.

Leila Osei

Occupational Therapist. Leila Osei specializes in ergonomic workplace evaluations and custom hand splint fittings. She helps patients adapt everyday activities to protect sensitive joints and reduce morning strain.

Samir Haddad

Pharmacist Liaison. Samir Haddad provides structured medication reviews and clinical liaison for systemic therapies. He advises patients on prescription schedules, monitoring protocols, and treatment tolerance.

Ruth Calloway

Reception and Scheduling Lead. Ruth Calloway oversees patient scheduling, intake diaries, and same-morning flare-day appointments. She coordinates clinic visits to ensure calm and timely access for every patient.

pages.title: Questions
pages.content:
Do I need a referral?

No. You can call us directly; if you have a referral letter or earlier results, bring them.

How do flare-day slots work?

Registered patients phone at 8:30 on the day; weekdays 8:30–9:30 and Saturday 8:30–9:00.

Do you give injections?

Yes, joint injections are done at the clinic, per joint, after an examination.

I am planning a pregnancy.

We will talk it through and coordinate with your obstetric team.

Can you write sick notes?

Yes, when they follow from an assessment we have made.

posts.title: The knuckle that stiffened overnight
posts.excerpt: Ana, 38, a cellist, from diary to first visit.
posts.content:
Ana noticed it on a Tuesday: the middle knuckle of her left hand was puffy and would not close around the bow until after her second coffee. It happened again on Thursday.

She phoned the clinic and was sent a one-page diary. For seven mornings she wrote down how long the stiffness lasted and which joints were swollen. That page was the first thing Dr. Achterberg read at the first visit.

The visit took an hour: history, a 28-joint examination, an ultrasound of both hands and bloods. Ten days later she came back to read and sign a one-page plan.

posts.title: Planning around a flare week
posts.excerpt: Peter, 61, a bus driver, how the flare-day slot and nurse line work.
posts.content:
Peter drives the number 14. When his wrists flare he cannot grip the wheel for the first hour, and a week of that is a problem for him and for his passengers.

His plan says what to do: phone at 8:30 for a flare-day slot, and speak to his named nurse, Ines, about adjusting medicine within the limits the plan sets.

He says the page on his fridge matters more than any single appointment. He knows who to call and what will be asked.

posts.title: What the twelve-week review is for
posts.excerpt: Hana, 45, a teacher, what is checked and why.
posts.content:
By week twelve there is enough history to see a pattern. Hana’s review started with her diary, then the same 28 joints that were examined at the first visit.

Bloods and, where useful, a repeat ultrasound show whether inflammation has settled. Her plan was adjusted, and the next review date was written on the page before she left.

Reviews at 4, 12 and 24 weeks are the early rhythm; after that, every three months.
